name: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis

possible: Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis (younger sexually active men — different management)
pathogens.why: Acute bacterial prostatitis in older men typically reflects the same uropathogens as other UTIs, ascending into the prostate; in younger sexually active men, sexually transmitted pathogens should specifically be considered as they require different antibiotic coverage and partner management.

investigations.why: Identifies the causative organism; this is preferred over prostatic secretion sampling in the acute setting given bacteremia risk with prostatic massage.
Bacteremia is not uncommon in acute prostatitis and positive cultures help confirm the organism.

investigations.test: Post-void residual / bladder scan (if retention suspected)
investigations.why: Urinary retention is a recognized complication requiring catheterization (suprapubic preferred over urethral if prostatitis is causing obstruction).

investigations.test: STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia) if risk factors present
investigations.why: Identifies sexually transmitted causes requiring different management and partner notification.

reasonSource: e=>`Lower urinary tract symptoms with ${[e.perinealPain&&"perineal/pelvic pain",e.feverGU&&"fever",e.urinaryRetention&&"urinary retention"].filter(Boolean).join(", ")||"pelvic symptoms"} in a male patient is consistent with acute bacterial prostatitis. Antibiotics with reliable prostatic tissue penetration are required, and digital rectal examination should be performed gently (vigorous prostatic massage is avoided in the acute setting due to bacteremia risk).`
